\boxed{65}

A set of 8 flags is diverse exactly when, for some color $c$, the flags can be perfectly matched to the 8 positions so that the flag matched to position $i$ shows color $c$ in field $i$. Hence a family $\mathcal F$ of flags contains no diverse subset iff for both colors the matching number $\nu_c(\mathcal F)\le 7$.

By Hall’s deficiency theorem, $\nu_c\le 7$ implies there is a nonempty set of positions $I_c$ with $|N_c(I_c)|\le |I_c|-1$, where $N_c(I)$ are the flags of $\mathcal F$ having color $c$ somewhere in $I$. Take such $I$ for blue and $J$ for yellow, with $a=|I|$, $b=|J|$.

Any flag outside $N_1(I)\cup N_0(J)$ is all-yellow on $I$ and all-blue on $J$. If $I\cap J\neq\varnothing$ this is impossible, so $|\mathcal F|\le a+b-2\le 14$. If $I\cap J=\varnothing$, then
$$|\mathcal F|\le (a-1)+(b-1)+2^{8-a-b}.$$
Maximizing over $a,b\ge1$, $a+b\le8$ gives $64$ at $a=b=1$.

Thus any family with no diverse set has at most $64$ flags. This bound is attained by all $64$ flags with field 1 yellow and field 2 blue (position 1 can never be blue, position 2 can never be yellow). Therefore $M=64+1=65$.

\boxed{65}

**Derivation.**  
Identify a flag with a binary vector in $\{0,1\}^8$ (0 = blue, 1 = yellow).  
Eight flags are diverse iff for some colour $c$ the bipartite graph between the $8$ positions and the $8$ flags (edge = the flag has colour $c$ at that position) contains a matching of size $8$.

If a family $\mathcal F$ contains **no** diverse $8$-set, then for each colour the matching number is $\le 7$. By König's theorem each colour graph has a vertex cover of size $\le7$:
- yellow cover: $a$ positions and $s$ flags, $a+s\le7$;
- blue cover: $b$ positions and $t$ flags, $b+t\le7$.

A flag outside both flag-covers must have all yellow positions inside the $a$ covered positions and all blue positions inside the $b$ covered positions; equivalently its yellow set $Y$ satisfies $[8]\setminus P_{\text{blue}}\subseteq Y\subseteq P_{\text{yellow}}$. This is possible only if $a+b\ge8$, and then there are at most $2^{a+b-8}$ such flags.

Hence
$$|\mathcal F|\le 2^{a+b-8}+s+t\le 2^{a+b-8}+14-(a+b)\le 64,$$
the last inequality maximised at $a=b=7$, $s=t=0$.

**Construction attaining 64:** fix two distinct positions, say require position $1$ yellow and position $8$ blue. The $2^6=64$ distinct flags obtained have no yellow at position $8$ and no blue at position $1$, so each colour graph uses at most $7$ positions and has matching number $\le7$; no diverse set exists.

Thus the largest family without a diverse $8$-set has size $64$, and $M=64+1=65$.

\boxed{65}

A set of 8 flags is diverse exactly when, in the bipartite graph between the flags and the 8 positions, the edges of one colour (blue or yellow) contain a perfect matching. Hence a family of flags contains **no** diverse 8-set iff both colour-graphs have matching number at most 7.

By König's theorem, the blue graph then has a vertex cover $A\cup B$ with $A$ among the flags, $B\subseteq[8]$, $|A|+|B|\le 7$; every flag outside $A$ has all its blue cells inside $B$, so there are at most $2^{|B|}$ such flags. Likewise the yellow graph yields a cover $A'\cup B'$ with $|A'|+|B'|\le 7$; writing $C=[8]\setminus B'$, every flag outside $A'$ contains $C$ and $|A'|\le |C|-1$.

If $C\not\subseteq B$ the family lies in $A\cup A'$, giving at most $(7-|B|)+(|C|-1)\le 9$ flags. If $C\subseteq B$, set $d=|B|-|C|\ge0$; then
$$|F|\le |A|+|A'|+2^{d}\le (7-|B|)+(|C|-1)+2^{d}=6-d+2^{d}\le 64,$$
the maximum occurring at $d=6$ (so $|B|=7$, $|C|=1$).

The bound is attained by the $2^6=64$ flags whose first field is blue and last field is yellow: position 1 is never yellow and position 8 is never blue, so no 8 of them can form a monochromatic diagonal. Thus the largest diverse-set-free family has size $64$, and $M=64+1=65$.
